description: We are Carrotly, a team of creative engineers from Poland at the Space Apps local event in Stalowa Wola. This year we are building a multiplayer browser game in which kids run a Mars base and face real mission trade-offs: air, food, water, power and radiation, based on real NASA data.
summary:
Marsonauts is a multiplayer browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. You land at a real spot on Mars, unload your lander and keep a small crewed base alive. Every sol you balance the trade-offs a real mission faces: oxygen, food from the pantry and the greenhouse, water from an ice drill, power from solar panels and batteries, muscles weakening in low gravity, and radiation from cosmic rays and solar storms.

The rules are built on real numbers instead of simplifications: the Sun stands where it really is over your landing site (NASA's Mars24 algorithm), the ground is real Mars from NASA Mars Trek (MOLA heights, Viking colours), and the radiation doses replay what Curiosity's RAD instrument measured on the surface. Kids learn by doing, through short plain-language messages and crewmates who explain each machine, and they can play together in one crew. When something goes wrong, the game shows why, so the next mission goes better.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Marsonauts puts kids in charge of a small crewed base on Mars. A rocket flies them from Earth, a lander sets them down at a real place on Mars, and their first mission is to unload it: supply crates go to the storage, nutrient packs and seeds go to the supply cabinet. That walk takes them through the whole base and introduces the crew. From then on they keep the base and themselves alive:

- Air: a suit holds 8 hours of oxygen; the airlock refills it. Oxygen for the base comes from a MOXIE-style oxygen maker, an electrolyser, and perchlorate heated in the lab furnace.

- Water: an ice drill fills 100 L water cans that carry the base's water; an electrolyser and a Sabatier reactor turn water and Mars CO2 into oxygen, hydrogen and methane fuel.

- Food: a pantry from Earth, a greenhouse with hydroponic trays and Mars-soil beds that must first be rinsed of toxic perchlorate, grow lamps, and a spirulina tank.

- Power: solar panels, a battery bank and portable power cells that machines run on; dust storms and night cut the power.

- Health: hunger, muscle loss in 38% gravity (train in the gym), and a radiation dosimeter. Cosmic rays add up every sol; solar storms are announced by the flare's light minutes before the protons arrive, and the crew shelters behind a wall of water cans.

- Research: from Mission Control the crew drives the Scout rover to a target, drills a rock core, analyses it in the lab and radios the results to Earth, waiting the real light-time delay for the answer.

WHY IT MATTERS

The challenge asks for the trade-offs of a real mission, made tangible and fun. Every resource here competes with another: water is drinking water, but also a radiation shield, a way to clean the soil, and the source of oxygen and fuel. Time outside costs suit oxygen and radiation dose. Power runs either the drill or the lamps. Kids feel these choices directly, and when the base fails, the game says why.

REAL DATA, NOT SIMPLIFICATIONS

- The ground: elevation from MOLA and colour from the Viking mosaic, streamed from NASA Mars Trek, so the whole planet is walkable.

- The Sun and the day: computed with the Mars24 algorithm for the real landing site, now; a sol lasts 24 h 39 min.

- Real robots stand where they really are: Curiosity and Perseverance from their published waypoints, plus the historic landing sites.

- Radiation: 0.64 mSv per sol of cosmic rays, as Curiosity's RAD measured on the surface, and two solar storms replayed from real events (September 2017 and May 2024, checked against NASA's DONKI database).

- Machines and crops use published numbers (MOXIE, ISS life support and the Veggie garden, Phoenix's perchlorate find).

MADE FOR KIDS

Short plain-language messages, crewmates who explain each machine when you talk to them, a short tutorial, footprints that show where to go, and big readable panels designed by our designer. Kids can play alone or with friends in one crew on the same Mars.
